·
第2️⃣天：一整天深度玩转阿尔山秋景，早起看不动河的晨雾，河流边还有牛牛和漫山遍野的金黄橙红交织，午后光线柔和林间光影刚好，随手拍出森系治愈大片
·
第3️⃣天：阿尔山前往呼伦湖再到满洲里住宿，沿途是满目鎏金秋色，中午抵达呼伦湖，秋日湖面澄澈静谧小羊门悠闲踱步，傍晚抵达满洲里，逛异域风情街头，吃地道的内蒙火锅
·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·
第6️⃣天：上午欣赏额尔古纳草原初秋的湿地黄绿渐变河道蜿蜒，成群的牛马过水美的不像话，下午奔赴莫日格勒河俯瞰天下第一曲水壮阔又温柔，在落日余晖下我们疯狂拍照记录下开心时刻，返回海拉尔吃了心心念念的俄餐
第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程

Day7：海拉尔→返程

items.title: The Industrial Revolution is the reason RPGs have area-of-effect spells: A PC Gamer Causality Chain™
items.author: Jody Macgregor
items.summary:
Causality Chain is a series at PC Gamer exploring the unlikely links between history, culture, and videogames.

Every time you cast a meteor spell in Diablo 2
items.text:
Causality Chain is a series at PC Gamer exploring the unlikely links between history, culture, and videogames.

Every time you cast a meteor spell in Diablo 2 or a cloud of daggers in Baldur's Gate 3, you are taking part in a chain of history—a causality chain, if you will—that dates back to the 18th century, when nobody had thought about taking a "warlock dip" since the Salem witch trials. And at that time, it had a very different meaning.

Today we trace the arc of history from the death of the agrarian period, all the way forward to that time you managed to set fire to five goblins at once and felt quite good about how clever you were. We chart the curious contours of cause and effect, and then we put our chins into our hands and we say, "Hmmm. Yes. This is good."

Join us as we tip the dominoes that link the past to the present, then watch the huge and intricate Rube Goldberg machine known as "history" fall over into a heap of discarded playing pieces.

The industrial revolution 🔗 Area-of-effect spells in RPGs

Rise of Industry

1760–1840: Technological advances including improvements to the steam engine and the viability of larger blast furnaces thanks to the substitution of coke for old-fashioned charcoal—combined with various other social and economic factors—radically changes daily life for many people. During this Industrial Revolution, skilled craftsmen are replaced by machine tools and the factory system becomes widespread.

Also the social policy trees for Order and Autocracy are unlocked, and we can finally research Dynamite, Electricity, and Refrigeration on the tech tree.

The Black Country

1896: J. R. R. Tolkien's family moves from Birmingham to rural Worcestershire. The four-year-old Tolkien discovers a love for the English countryside that will later inform his writing. His aunt's farm, Bag End, gives its name to the Baggins' home, and places like Moseley Bog in Shire Country Park inspire the Old Forest in the Shire.

"It was a kind of lost paradise," he will later tell a journalist in his first newspaper interview. It was an area that had survived industrialization—though not for long. As he says in an introduction to the second edition of The Lord of the Rings:

"The country in which I lived in childhood was being shabbily destroyed before I was ten, in days when motorcars were still rare objects (I had never seen one) and men were still building suburban railways. Recently I saw in a paper a picture of the last decrepitude of the once thriving corn-mill beside its pool that long ago seemed to me so important."

(Image credit: Monolith Productions, WB Games)The soot-darkened countryside of the formerly green Midlands is known as the Black Country to this day. In her novel How to Build a Girl, Caitlin Moran has a working-class Midlands man explain the change to his literate daughter:

"When I was a kid, you'd come up this hill, and all of that –" and he gestures to the valley in front of us "– was on fire. The foundries and the forges and the ironworks. The potteries. The whole place glowed – sheets of sparks, fifty foot high. The fires never went out. It looked like hell. Mordor. That's what your Lord of the Rings is about. Tolkien was from round here. He was writing about how the Industrial Revolution turned the Midlands from Hobbiton into Mordor."

Mordor, in Tolkien's invented language Sindarin, means "the Black Land".

The Devilry of Saruman

1954: The Lord of the Rings is published. Tolkien's wizards embody his feelings about industrialization. Saruman, who turns to evil, constructs smoke-billowing factories around the tower of Orthanc and later in Hobbiton itself, and uses magical fire in the creation of an explosive substance that can knock down walls ("they have lit the fire of Orthanc", as Aragorn puts it during the Battle of the Hornburg).

Meanwhile, Gandalf uses his magic to create pretty fireworks. He's capable of more—as he tells the Balrog, "I am a servant of the Secret Fire, wielder of the flame of Anor." Yet time and again he prefers subtlety to explosions. Though his burning pine cones frighten away wolves in The Hobbit, and in The Lord of the Rings he uses magical flame when the Fellowship is attacked while making camp on its way to Moria, both times he has cause to regret it.

Fire of Wrath

(Image credit: New Line Cinema)1970: And yet, perhaps because Gandalf uses magical fire rarely and dramatically, it ends up being cemented as a thing he does in the mind of at least one wargamer. Leonard Patt's Rules for Middle Earth, developed for the New England Wargamers Association, are published in their zine The Courier and end up influencing game designers for decades to come.

How does Patt model Gandalf's magical fire in a wargame? He treats it like artillery. Patt's description of the "fire ball" is the first depiction of a magical spell with an area-of-effect rule, and incidentally the first appearance of a saving throw:

"Wizards in possession of magic powers can cast a fire ball once every other turn. The distance is 24" and the hit is determined by using a 6" grid with a 2½" burst circle. Any figures under the burst are killed except HEROES nad [sic] ANTI-HEROES, who are saved by a throw of a 5 or 6."

Backdraft

(Image credit: James Oorloff Photography)1974: Dungeons & Dragons is published by TSR. The work of Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson, its rules build on the fantasy supplement for the Chainmail wargame by Gygax and Jeff Perren, which built on Patt's Rules for Middle Earth.

The fireball spell has a burst radius of 2" in original Dungeons & Dragons, which translates to 20 feet if you're not playing with miniatures, and will "conform to the shape of the space", meaning that it can blow back if cast into a small dungeon room—a rule that led to the death of many 5th-level magic users.

Screen Burn

1975: University student Daniel Lawrence converts D&D to digital form on a PDP-10 mainframe computer. Initially called DND, though later renamed Telengard for a commercial release, it's one of the first videogame RPGs and it does contain a fireball spell. There's no area of effect, however, as all combat in DND/Telengard is one-on-one.

Friendly Fire

(Image credit: Origin Systems)The 1980s: Early videogames simulate area-of-effect in various ways. The Wizardry games have spells that target half or all of the enemies in a given group, and Ultima 3's noxum spell lets you cast multiple fireballs, each targeting a separate individual.

In 1985, Ultima 4's tremor spell affects every enemy on screen. Wizard's Crown in 1986 has a fireball that affects enemies in the squares around its target, and 1988's Ultima 5 adds cone-shaped spells.

That same year SSI, developer of Wizard's Crown, picks up the licence to make official D&D games and releases Pool of Radiance. The first RPG in the Gold Box series, it uses the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 1st edition rules, complete with a true area-of-effect fireball spell that can easily cook your own party members if you're not careful—just like Tolkien warned us would happen.

items.title: Halo needed to change, but Activision faces a huge challenge to fix it
items.author: morgan.park@futurenet.com (Morgan Park)
items.summary: Microsoft has given up on Halo Studios, the team it formed and recently renamed for the express purpose of making new Halo games. Another victim of the Xbox
items.text:
Microsoft has given up on Halo Studios, the team it formed and recently renamed for the express purpose of making new Halo games. Another victim of the Xbox Reset, the studio has been slashed down to its bones as part of another (but not final) wave of layoffs, and what's left of Halo Studios will now oversee the franchise in nebulous-sounding ways. Indeed: Halo Studios is no longer making Halo.

Now Activision is in charge, and as both a Halo and Call of Duty fan, the pairing isn't exciting.

Though I've been a vocal critic of Halo Studios' take on Halo over the years ("Halo Studios has no discernably new take on Bungie's landmark FPS" -Me, 2026), Halo Infinite eventually grew into a strong multiplayer FPS that I sunk hundreds of hours into, and Halo: Campaign Evolved was the team's best effort yet to embrace the series' quirky traditions while keeping an eye toward evolution. Ripping that work away from them a few months after shipping a Halo remake is a drastic move.

Let's take a moment to account for Halo Studios' history.

What Halo Studios got right, in my eyes

Core Halo multiplayer was in tact: 4v4 arena modes and Big Team Battle

Art: By Infinite, the studio had found a striking art direction for Halo, and Spartans looked amazing.

Gunplay: Especially in Infinite, Halo Studios raised the bar for the series

Maps: Halo maps remained strange, asymmetrical battlegrounds suited for floaty physics

Forge: Halo's level creator was so powerful enough by Infinite that the community was making minigames and maps good enough to enter the official rotation

And where Halo Studios often got it wrong

Campaigns: We spent two games shooting at Prometheans, which were like Covenant but worse

Story: They took Master Chief way too seriously and turned him into a hero of destiny, and somehow made him uncool

Unpopular experiments: Halo became a testbed for every multiplayer trend of the last decade-plus (create-a-class, loot boxes, battle passes, even MOBA-like modes), which gave every new game an identity crisis

Timing: Halo Studios struggled to make Halo with regularity. There was a six-year gap between Halo 5 and Infinite, then another five years before Halo: Campaign Evolved.

You can see why Microsoft thinks Activision is suited to fix some of those mistakes—Call of Duty can still produce a decent campaign. While the industry struggles with longer development cycles, Activision has maintained a steady pace.

That pace has come with real compromise—like never knowing if this year's CoD will be embarrassingly bad or merely good enough—and that's why I question if it'll be a worthy steward for what was once among the most celebrated and unique shooters in history. Despite its shortcomings, Halo Infinite stood out by doing things differently than Call of Duty with a slower pace, hipfiring guns, mirrored loadouts, power weapons, and vertical maps that had more in common with classic arena shooters than the 'boots on the ground' generation that Modern Warfare created.

I don't think that the outcome of this is going to be Halo becoming more Call of Duty-like, but I don't trust the Call of Duty machine to be a good influence on Halo, especially as Activision juggles two titanic franchises simultaneously.

343 IndustriesActivision BlizzardNo doubt that Activision is eager to put Halo back on the map, but I hope they'll be able to match the attention to detail of the Halo Studios staffers that Microsoft just fired. Say what you will of their final products, but they were massive fans of Halo: This is the studio that didn't stop improving The Master Chief Collection until it was a gold standard of preservation; the studio that allowed community members to rummage through the records and publish an unfinished Halo 2 E3 demo on Steam Workshop; that cared enough about the minutiae of Halo's jump physics and grenade bounces to literally run 15-year-old Halo Reach code under the hood of Campaign Evolved.

Activision will be put in a very challenging creative position: presumably to put some new spin on Halo that will work better than the last few releases, but also to earn fans' trust by preserving whatever aspects of the franchise it deems sacred. How will that play out? Call of Duty is famous for changing up its setting, tone, characters, and gameplay as it bounces from studio to studio. Fans have adapted to the whiplash over the years, but the series' inconsistent identity is a tradeoff that Activision either accepts as part of cranking out annual releases or has chosen to embrace. I don't want something similar to happen to Halo as its makers seek to restore its relevance.

Because honestly, the things I love most about Halo—its streamlined weapon sandbox, emphasis on vehicles, uncomplicated modes, social lobbies, and community-driven custom games—aren't in vogue anymore. If the goal is to transform Halo into one of the most-played multiplayer shooters in the world, I'm just not sure how a studio achieves that while simultaneously preserving what makes Halo great, 25 years later.

items.text:
For the time being, DLSS5 is only officially available via Nvidia's 50-series cards. The company has said in the past the neural rendering tech will eventually come to 40-series cards too, but I simply couldn't wait. Having now witnessed multiple passes of the upscaling tech applied to my anime-style game of choice, I have some regrets.

To be clear, the only way to get DLSS5 working with my Nvidia RTX 4070 Super is through completely unofficial means. You can scour the internet for the files you need, though there are some software options that automate the process.

For this unholy experiment, I used DLSS5 Manager and went to town with its adjustable 'Live Flow' function.

My game of choice for this unsanctioned exercise is Hatsune Miku: Project Diva Mega Mix+. This game has an anime-adjacent art style that DLSS 5 has no business upscaling, but I'm not letting that stop me. Before finagling a way to apply DLSS5 to this game, it ran at a fairly solid 60 fps (though that's a best case scenario largely dependent on which song you're playing—if you're a Project Diva sicko, you know what I mean).

With Live Flow active, my frame rate tanked to the point that pressing timed button prompts became almost impossible.

Thankfully, Project Diva lets you watch all of its music videos without the rhythm mechanics getting in the way to remind you that you've got no sense of timing to begin with. From the main in-game menu I selected 'Custom Playlists,' composed a music video running order, and then headed off to the deepest pits of neural rendering Hell.

Oh, I have such sights to show you. Take a look at some of my comparisons below.

blocks.x: For the time being, DLSS5 is only officially available via Nvidia's 50-series cards. The company has said in the past the neural rendering tech will eventually come to 40-series cards too, but I simply couldn't wait. Having now witnessed multiple passes of the upscaling tech applied to my anime-style game of choice, I have some regrets.

To be clear, the only way to get DLSS5 working with my Nvidia RTX 4070 Super is through completely unofficial means. You can scour the internet for the files you need, though there are some software options that automate the process.
For this unholy experiment, I used DLSS5 Manager and went to town with its adjustable 'Live Flow' function.

My game of choice for this unsanctioned exercise is Hatsune Miku: Project Diva Mega Mix+. This game has an anime-adjacent art style that DLSS 5 has no business upscaling, but I'm not letting that stop me. Before finagling a way to apply DLSS5 to this game, it ran at a fairly solid 60 fps (though that's a best case scenario largely dependent on which song you're playing—if you're a Project Diva sicko, you know what I mean).
With Live Flow active, my frame rate tanked to the point that pressing timed button prompts became almost impossible.

Thankfully, Project Diva lets you watch all of its music videos without the rhythm mechanics getting in the way to remind you that you've got no sense of timing to begin with. From the main in-game menu I selected 'Custom Playlists,' composed a music video running order, and then headed off to the deepest pits of neural rendering Hell.

items.title: Bethesda say new underlings Obsidian will retain their "distinct" creative identity, despite no longer being as free to work on their own creatively distinct series
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: Obsidian will remain a "distinct" Obsidian with their own "creative identity and strengths", despite no longer operating independently of fellow Xbox-owned RPG
items.text:
Obsidian will remain a "distinct" Obsidian with their own "creative identity and strengths", despite no longer operating independently of fellow Xbox-owned RPG makers Bethesda. That's according to Jill Braff, president of Bethesda and Microsoft's casual games division, in a memo sent to staff at the former following this week's layoffs and reorganising of studios at Xbox.

"Obsidian has extraordinary creative talent, deep expertise, and a long history of creating memorable games and experiences," the exec wrote in the memo, which has been published by IGN. "I’m looking forward to working more closely with them. Today’s announcement is primarily a change in reporting structure. The creative identity and strengths that make Obsidian distinct will remain at the core of their studio and work.

"[CEO] Feargus [Urquhart] and the Obsidian leadership team will continue to lead Obsidian, with the studio reporting to me. Bethesda Game Studios will continue to lead the Fallout franchise. Together, the teams will build on their longstanding relationship and the early work already underway on a new Fallout project, with more to share in the months ahead. This structure supports the franchise-led model we’ve been strengthening while keeping accountability for both the studio and the franchise clear."

Braff added that this isn't a case of the company "resetting [their] roadmap or asking teams to change what they’re focused on", and that they'll instead "take the time to understand how teams can best support one another, and where closer partnership can benefit our players and fans".

To be fair, that switch in focus already happened for at least some of Obsidian's remaining devs prior to this week's cuts, with them being put to work on that new Fallout game helmed by New Vegas director Josh Sawyer. Obsidian's own RPG series, The Outer Worlds and Avowed, look to have gone thoroughly on the backburner as part of the shift.

It's very difficult to see how Xbox can have and eat the cake Braff describes. The distinct identity the exec celebrates in the memo exists because of Obsidian's previous independence. If they can't work on their own unique game series without the boss of another game studio with its own long-established creative identity perched atop them, it's more likely they'll morph into a collaborator, simply supporting Bethesda's series. That second outcome would better fit the mould Xbox are adopting, in which they're rallying around a small number of well-established big hitter game series.

At best, enough of that distinct Obsidian identity is allowed to be retained that the Fallout game the studio have in the works is as much of a yin to Bethesda's wasteland-crafting yang as New Vegas was all those years ago. But even then, there doesn't seem like there'll be room to play to other strengths and creative strong points to foster series that could be part of the next generation of RPG hits. If swings on The Outer Worlds and Avowed appear unlikely, we're almost certainly not getting another esoteric, small-scale RPG like Pentiment. Fallout and The Elder Scrolls didn't build their vast reputations and mass appeal overnight. There's also more pressure on both series now than ever before: Xbox appear to be enshrining them saviours that will carry the wider company wherever their bosses decide they want them to go.

To torture a Fallout metaphor a bit, a town previously just within NCR or Legion-controlled territory simply won't be as free if either faction stations a garrison right in the middle of it. items.title: The scariest part of Silent Hill: Townfall? It's not the monsters—it's British interior design
items.author: Samuel Roberts
items.summary: Silent Hill: Townfall has a different kind of resonance if you grew up in the UK. Its Scottish island of St Amelia is already my favourite video game
items.text:
Silent Hill: Townfall has a different kind of resonance if you grew up in the UK. Its Scottish island of St Amelia is already my favourite video game environment of the year for how it evokes the atmosphere and time of a place—specifically 1996—and captures the specific details of small town life.

From the video rental shop to the bunting sadly hanging from the buildings, it's the kind of run-down fishing town you never normally see in a video game. That's probably because it's not as glamorous as somewhere like Kamurocho in Tokyo (St Amelia regrettably lacks a Sega World) or New York, and not as dreamy as the Stephen King-inflected small town settings of games like Alan Wake or Silent Hill 2.

Using the Silent Hill franchise as this trojan horse to smuggle in a location that's clearly of interest to the Glasgow-based development team at Screen Burn was a marvellous idea: given the state of the games industry, it's unlikely that anyone will ever again be given the budget or time to craft an authentic British newsagent or storefront for a fish and chip shop.

Still, as eerily authentic as St Amelia's exterior details are, like the telephone boxes and road signs, it's the interiors that I find uniquely settling. Here's why: my grandparents basically lived in the houses in this game.

Konami/Screen BurnKonami/Screen BurnKonami/Screen BurnThe kitchen tiling, the heaters, the wallpaper, the appliances—it's so forensically accurate to a certain type of house. The kind of places that were last renovated in the '70s or '80s and haven't been touched since, maybe because the residents were too old to want to redecorate or because they couldn't afford to do so. When I step into these homes in Silent Hill: Townfall, my gut response is, "I've been here before and I hate it."

'70s chic

The artists at Screen Burn didn't just capture 1996 in some of these homes, they pinpointed the environmental details that were old even then. That's next level visual craft, assisted by things like ancient Argos catalogues.

"Some genius out there had scanned every Argos catalogue for the last 30 years," game director Jon McKellan told us at Gamescom, "and we were like looking at them and finding out, OK, if we need a TV in '90s, let's look at the catalogue from the '90s and find out which one would be more appropriate."

I sent the above screenshots to my mum. "That is my parents’ house," she confirmed about the first two images, talking about a terrace house somewhere in the midlands. "We all huddled round that gas fire."

To me and many other British players there will be an extra nightmarish layer to the game because of this familiarity. Seeing a world that you know you've visited before but that is now totally lost is uniquely unsettling.

Why am I fixated on this? Well, I have encountered this feeling of nostalgic spookiness before when I've watched old British TV stuff like the ultra-cursed Tales of the Unexpected or Threads, but never in a game.

Maybe the game's 1996 setting is just to satisfy director Jon McKellan's love of analogue tech, which is similarly front-and-centre in the likes of Stories Untold and Alien: Isolation, but these interiors feel like the result of a hundred artistic choices.

That specificity in the environmental design, to me, is quietly the best thing about Silent Hill: Townfall (with apologies to the actual game bit, which I am enjoying even if I'm swearing at the stealth sections a whole lot).

I've brightened this screenshot just to highlight the terror of a '00s phone box. (Image credit: Konami/Screen Burn)Even the likes of Everybody's Gone to the Rapture or Atomfall tend to romanticise elements of British life in their countryside locations. Silent Hill: Townfall blots out any potential warmth of these empty houses by surrounding them with fog, towering walls and monsters, and making them the backdrop for a gnarly psychological horror story.

Still Wakes the Deep got a bit closer to this feeling, being a '70s period piece set off the coast of Scotland—but that took place on an oil rig, and living on one of those isn't exactly a universal experience.

The thing is, to my parents' generation, the types of houses you explore in Townfall are just the places they grew up in. My mum says she finds '70s interior design quite warm and comforting. This clicked something else into place for me about why I find these details frightening: it's probably just an age thing.

(Image credit: Konami)When I watched this year's mega hit film Backrooms, I came out of it wondering why the children all found it so frightening. I'm doomed to know the concept of a 'liminal space' from the amount of time I spend online, of course, but what they seemed to be afraid of was basically an empty Woolworths retail unit.

I get that any empty space that's supposed to have people in it can be quite eerie, but the basis of an entire online mythology and $400 million movie? That was strange to me. But that's really a younger audience's version of what I'm experiencing here.

My theory is, whatever ordinary place seems old to you is inherently unsettling. The things that we find normal now will seem otherworldly, grim and strange to future generations.

One day, someone will make a horror game set in a strip mall with a gorgeously rendered bubble tea shop, vape shop and Apple Store. And to me, it won't be a horror game at all. It'll be a documentary.

items.title: Microsoft want to record your face and feed it to a generative AI, telling it to go off and design a game from your frown
items.author: Julian Benson
items.summary: A new patent from Microsoft shows how they want to record your facial expressions, show them to an AI, and have it redesign the game you're playing. It's not
items.text:
A new patent from Microsoft shows how they want to record your facial expressions, show them to an AI, and have it redesign the game you're playing. It's not only your face they want, but also any words you might be muttering, growls you might be making, or, dare I say, even purrs.

The broader technology described in the patent is a process for game designers to prompt an AI to build out the narrative elements of a game, including objectives, sidequests, NPCs, dialogue, and items. Rather than stop at that first pass, the process would continue when players are in the game, analysing how they're playing to then generate new content based on their actions and reactions.

A quick peek behind the curtain: I, too, am using this technology and the rest of this article has been rewritten to match exactly the facial expression you are making right… now.

US patent 20260183672A1, pithily titled Generative Narrative Game Experience With Player Feedback, doesn't describe a technology Microsoft have already made – it is more a case of describing a process of how this tech would work if they were to make it. As ever with patent documents, they are as much a case of laying the groundwork to say "I thought of that first" to a judge when one of your competitors does a thing, as much as they are something you actually intend to do. They also often have the quality of talking to a child describing the spaceship they would make if they were given half the chance – "...and its legs have pipes filled with jelly, so when it lands it can turn the ground into trampolines". As such, you can't read a patent document as the company has done a thing so much as the company has thought about doing a thing.

Anyway, onto the thing Microsoft wants everyone to know they have thought about.

The patent describes a few ways the process would work. In one, it's predominantly on the dev side. The patent suggests that a designer could prompt an AI, using written input, images, and audio files, and the engine would then create characters, narratives, and worlds "at a high level" that the designer would finesse. That finessing would either be by directly editing what the model created or by giving it more prompts to refine what was in front of them. Once the designer was happy with what they had made, they could implement it within a game.

The authors suggest the prompt could be "merely a general theme, idea, or goal for the game or characterize the general nature of the game, or it may include some narrative details, such as main characters, a basic storyline, etc." The model would then go on to create game content – NPCs, items, dialogue, lore descriptions, and objectives and sidequests. This would then be given back to the designer as "a visual representation of the game [...] in the form of text, images, and/or graphs".

Personally, I find the vagueness here delightful. All I can picture is the creators of Deep Thought, the massive supercomputer in the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, prompting the machine for the answer to the ultimate question: Life! The Universe! Everything! And receiving the answer 42. I can imagine a designer sitting at their desktop, writing 'Computer, build me a game about the theme of grief', only to be presented with a flowchart 'Main character loves person > loved person dies > Main character = sad". Thank you, computer.

The patent does go on to say that along with the visual representation, the model may also provide code you can stick into a game engine. Alternatively, they say an already existing game, such as Minecraft, could be updated with new content via an api. Well, that all sounds marvellously simple.

Another way the tech would work is for that design role to be taken up by the player – though, not through direct prompting, as with the designer, but with an AI adapting the world based on the player's actions and "engagement metrics". In this example, it's not something that happens on the fly as you're playing, but either while the game is still in development or between release builds. So, for instance, the players would be QA testers, beta testers, or early access players. Data would be collected from their play and fed into the model and it would spit out content for a designer to work with before officially incorporating it into the game.

Though, they also then go on to describe interactions which are very much on-the-fly calls to a generative AI, similar to the conversations we've seen players have with NPCs in games like Where Winds Meet. The patent's authors say that the model would take what a player asked an NPC, along with contextual information such as where they are in the game, what they've been talking about with other NPCs, and the story path they've taken in the game, and stuff that into a generative AI to come up with a response. They excitedly write, "the possible natural-language output of the conversational agent are virtually limitless."

We have spoken to narrative directors in the past and they are less convinced…

Though Microsoft's engineers aren't just describing an NPC that spouts newly generated dialogue. They suggest taking the whole thing a little further. "an agent associated with an NPC may create not only conversational output (e.g., suggesting a side quest for the player to pursue), but also programmatic output that creates new game assets, rules, or alterations of the game world associated with the conversational output (e.g., objects or locations associated with the suggested side quest)." A new goal for me in any Microsoft game that allows me to speak directly to NPCs is going to be a two-hour attempt to convince them to turn off the world's gravity.

Outside of NPCs, the authors suggest that generative agents could operate other objects in the game. They use the example of a box that, instead of being unlocked with a key, is kicked open by the player. "In some instances, the new content can be so involved as to affect even the game narrative, creating new narrative elements, paths through the game, and modes of gameplay. In multi-player games, in particular, the collective interactions of players with each other and with the game can result in complex emergent new game behaviors."

Perhaps one day, I will kick open a box, a nearby NPC will begin to weep because the box was gift to them from their child. They will generate a sidequest where I go and apologise to their child and, as a reward for my efforts, they will turn the gravity off.

I really have to stress again at this point that there is no evidence that Microsoft have made any of this. They're not patenting a technology that exists in the world. This is basically a big 'Wouldn't it be cool off tech could do this? And, if anyone else does it first, we get the right to sue them for stealing our neat ideas wot we wrote down first.'

Other data Microsoft say they could scrape from a player's game is how often they return to an area, how long they spend talking to an NPC, whether they complete or abandon a quest. This isn't much different from how human game developers work, they also monitor how players move through their worlds and then make changes based off what they see. For instance, in Unreal Engine, you can collate movement data from tonnes of playtests and generate a heatmap to see where most players spent their time. It's just, at the other end of that, a human makes the decision of how to change the game.

The patent starts to get decidedly creepy when Microsoft suggests that "with permission" they could use cameras and microphones to "infer such indicators from the player's spoken comments, facial expressions, etc. during gameplay". They also suggest processing "live streams posted online" and feeding that into the AI model to make changes. This does raise the prospect that you could tell a game to delete itself and it would actually go off and do just that.

As you would expect, the dream of the people authoring this patent is that the game-designing AI would make more of what players like and less of what they didn't. "If a particular part of the game tends to attract players, the model may decide to elaborate on and extend that part of the game to further enhance player engagement. On the other end of the spectrum, game content that is less engaging, whether part of the original game or added on the fly, may be pruned or assigned lower weight."

Put another way, the AI might see the shocked and saddened faces of players during Aerith's death in Final Fantasy 7 and decide to delete the sequence, replacing it with something that makes them visibly happier. Or, recognising the emotional impact of the character's demise, opt to extend it for maximum effect, creating the All Too Well (10 Minute Version) of her final moments.

If you're now decidedly worried about what this AI generated future of video games looks like, there is some solace in the patent document. The authors provide an example of what an AI might suggest to a designer making a Wizard of Oz game. One suggested quest is "Complete the Wizard's Tasks: Once Dorothy reaches the Wizard's castle, they will be given a set of tasks to complete before the Wizard will grant them an audience. These tasks involve finding and collecting various items from around the land of Oz." That's hardly earth-shattering stuff. With insights like that, Lies of P developer Neowiz, who are currently hard at work at Oz-set Wonders of O, must be quaking in the boots.

So, in summary, Microsoft haven't made a thing, but they've stated how they would make a thing, and if they do make that thing, then you may want to start wearing a mask when playing Microsoft games out of fear that should you pick your nose while play the game may add a section where you go digging for gold in a cave full of bats.

items.title: Unlike its stars, Brothers is only half-baked
items.author: Erik Adams
items.summary: If streaming-TV originals have a final form, it may be this: Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey playing fictionalized versions of themselves in what has
items.text:
If streaming-TV originals have a final form, it may be this: Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey playing fictionalized versions of themselves in what has to be the most expensive version of a 2010s ABC family sitcom ever made. An amusing-enough method of keeping Apple TV subscribers around between seasons of Ted Lasso and Stick, Brothers re-teams the-real life buds and True Detective stars in an alternately wholesome and profane Apple TV series that’s built around a tabloid anecdote and drafts off public personae the headlining talent previously plied in service of AI enterprise software.


Brothers’ laidback approach to telling the story of the Harrelson clan crashing at the McConaughey family ranch is held together by valiant efforts by some of the producers, writers, and directors behind the American Office, Modern Family, and New Girl. And yet when the sporadic laughter subsides, it’s hard not to see this celebrity-driven trifle as an indicator of the current state of TV that’s more accurate than any of the many awards Apple picked up during the night when the (possibly biological?) brothers of Brothers tried to get a rushed Emmys ceremony to the end of its timeslot through the sheer force of their combined charisma. And that’s all before self-anointed new king of Hollywood David Ellison’s name shows up in the credits.


Brothers is—per a title card that gets less cute and necessary (because who jumps into a streaming show midseason?) by the episode— “based on a true rumor” of a sexual encounter between Harrelson’s ne’er-do-well father and McConaughey’s mother (played here with plenty of southern-fried pluck by Holland Taylor). But the mystery of the Oscar winner’s paternity is mere logline window dressing for a show that’s more about the colliding worlds of two families and how those collisions prove that the bond of co-starring in Surfer, Dude is thicker than blood. It’s also, to varying degrees, a show about eldest Harrelson daughter Olive (Highdee Kuan) getting over a called-off engagement, her dad paying for the sins of his old man, and McConaughey making good on his idle thoughts of running for political office. The third of those plot lines is the most forced and farthest fetched, but it at least makes room for Lisa Gilroy to sprinkle a little Comedy Bang! Bang! weirdness into the proceedings as a high-strung campaign manager who upbraids Harrison and McConaughey in terms that, fortunately for Brothers, only kinda sorta encapsulate the show: “an endless barrage of egomaniacal and borderline sociopathic behavior from both of you.”


This is no vanity project. The leads allow themselves to look plenty foolish—particularly Harrelson, whose just slightly exaggerated personal beliefs and hippie-dippy flakiness make him a thorn in everyone on the ranch’s side. This also gives him a chance to tap into the comedic spirit of the last TV character he played who shared his first name; the golden retriever Woody Boyd energy that so frequently bolsters his performance here is a nice reminder that before Harrelson played hard-asses, deadbeats, and loose cannons on the big screen, he was one of the funniest supporting sitcom players of the ’80s. If nothing else Brothers is a fresh display of those particular talents.


Playing relatively straight man to the nomadic vegan bestie living out of the psychedelic bus in his driveway, McConaughey gets less color to play here. That’s in keeping with the poet-philosopher guise he’s donned since TV audiences first fell under the sway of Rust Cohle and his Big Hug Mug (a prop that’s too prominently displayed throughout Brothers to count as an Easter egg). But McConaughey’s corner of Brothers is more muted as a result, creating added strain for the campaign storyline, which, despite its Texas-size scale, lacks the more captivating personal stakes of what’s happening among the Harrelsons. McConaughey gets to cut loose in a few episodes with the Woodman, but of the two of them, he’s the one whose commitment to playing “himself” comes across as coasting.


Brothers lives in a hazy no-man’s land between “working vacation for movie stars” and “bingeable crowd-pleaser.” This is no slapdash production. The visuals capitalize on the natural splendor of the show’s Texas Hill Country setting; showrunner Lee Eisenberg hired plenty of names that will ring a bell for anyone who kept up with the vintage of network sitcom that Brothers most closely resembles. Between directors Trent O’Donnell, Erin O’Malley, and Jason Winer and writers Brett Baer, Dave Finkel, Alex Cuthbertson, and Matt Fusfeld, it feels like Eisenberg called his way down a New Girl alumni phone tree. (KPop Demon Hunters screenwriters Danya Jimenez and Hannah McMechan are aboard here too—for the most music-heavy episodes, naturally.) Every once in awhile, the experience in that writer’s room comes through loud and clear, as when Harrelson exchanges rat-a-tat with two old-timers trying to collect on a debt owed to them by his dad, or in a visual gag that reveals McConaughey’s incredibly involved grooming routines. Unfortunately, such material was placed in some run-of-the-mill scripts, with stock plots like Harrelson and McConaughey forgetting Valentine’s Day and paying a steep price for it.


Despite recalling comedies of days gone by, Brothers winds up feeling extremely contemporary—in mostly unflattering ways. It’s queue-filler of the highest order—TV-like product with megastar wattage. The half-hour episodes go down as easy as the craft brews McConaughey holds so conspicuously label-to-camera, but they lead to neither drunken comedic euphoria or regrettable “I can’t believe I watched the whole thing” hangover. There are some earnest attempts at fleshing out various family members and relationships—Harrelson and Kuan strike up a real tender dynamic while the scuttlebutt about Olive’s granddad and Ma Mac provides welcome distraction from her romantic woes. But there’s little sense of whether all that’s being developed there might continue to develop, or be worth developing, past this single season.


It’s not always funny, but Brothers is never not a curious artifact of an uneasy period in TV history, when one show can contain abundant f-bombs, some of the biggest bong rips ever put on television, and an adorable moppet putting her confidence to the test as she follows in her father’s footsteps and goes out for the school play. Yet as momentous as such events may be, there’s little sense of any of it impacting the characters in meaningful, long-lasting ways. To paraphrase the tagline for a movie whose iconography Brothers raids without shame or real thought (nobody raised an eyebrow at the sixth-episode school-dance invitation conducted in Wooderson cosplay?): We’re watching a time the fake Harrelsons and fake McConaugheys will never forget. If only we could remember anything about the show two or three months from now.


Erik Adams is The A.V. Club’s senior TV editor.

items.title: Prebuilt Steam Machine faceplate screens are here, delivering decent, surprisingly cheaper alternatives to Valve-approved DIY builds
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: If you own a Steam Machine, and still cling to the misconception that my budget faceplate ideas aren’t good enough for you, you basically have three options
items.text:
If you own a Steam Machine, and still cling to the misconception that my budget faceplate ideas aren’t good enough for you, you basically have three options for front panel customisation. The first is to grab something off Etsy or suchlike. The second is take advantage of Valve’s open-source Inkterface project to build yourself an E-Ink display, onto which you can electronically daub performance monitoring info. The third is to end up with more or less the same panel as option two, but have someone else make it for you. That’s what arch accessory makers JSAUX are proposing with their Steam Machine E-Ink and Pixel Matrix faceplates, which go on sale today after a few weeks of preening around the case mod scene.

I’ve been using both on my Machine at home, and they’re quite good fun. The E-Ink faceplate, for which I sense the greater internet buzz, is a crisp, tidy little black-and-white panel, while the PixelMatrix trades detail density for colour and retro charm. Both have a few different display modes, switchable in SteamOS’s quick settings menu (via some clever integration with the Decky Loader plugin tool), and while I had to set this up manually, JSAUX say the requisite software will be downloadable via Steam itself from early October. Truly, it’s all the results of a DIY mod and more, conveniently pre-prepared for people who don’t own soldering irons.

Of the two, I narrowly prefer the PixelMatrix, that favouritism expanding significantly when using a faceplate for performance monitoring. The E-Ink model is pretty knackered in this respect, as its fastest refresh speed option is a hardly widowmaking once per minute, and I’m rarely interested in what my Steam Machine’s GPU was doing sixty seconds ago. I also, uh, like how the sun is actually yellow on the PixelMatrix’s weather view. This is apparently what RPS hardware coverage has come to.

Tell you what, here’s a cat picture. One advantage the E-Ink screen has over the dot matrix is that it makes much, much more sense for turning the Steam Machine into a digital photo frame; this holiday snap of a stray Baku resident was just too detailed for the PixelMatrix’s chunky LEDs to recognisably reproduce. The latter might work for pics of your favourite Jenga block, or perhaps an ironic, front-on photo of the Steam Machine itself, but for anything with eyes or hair you’re better off with the E-Ink.

Granted, this isn’t the only shortcoming. I find it disproportionately annoying that the outer edges – on both faceplates – don’t quite line up perfectly with the USB/power button/ light strip section on the Machine’s bottom lip, and the right-sided USB-C port on the E-Ink panel forces the connecting cable to stretch unattractively across the same section. The FPS 'counter' on each screen’s performance monitors also downright misleads: it displays your TV/monitor’s refresh rate, in frames-per-second instead of Hz, and not actual in-game performance. It wouldn’t be very useful to get a once-per-minute framerate update on the E-Ink model anyway, but still.

At least when the E-Ink screen does refresh, though, it does so faster and less distractingly than Valve’s Inkterface design. A design which, if you follow the instructions by the book, will also give you a single performance monitoring screen, not the choice of performance, play time tracking, clock, weather, calendar, or photo frame modes that JSAUX’s ready-made screens have out of the box. And, in a major break from PC hardware convention, they both work out cheaper than taking the DIY option.

Now, "cheaper" doesn’t necessarily mean "cheap" - the E-Ink is $100 and the PixelMatrix is $90, or roughly a tenth of the infamously ‘spenny Machine it latches onto. These are undoubtedly luxuries, for those who didn’t already blow their entire luxury budget on miniature PCs. Yet totting up the combined component prices of what you’d need for an Inkerface panel reveals it to cost $104.50, not including the expense of either 3D-printing the external housing or buying something pre-printed for an additional 15 dollaridoos.

In a sense, then, the $100, sub-6in greyscale screen that only refreshes once a minute is... good value. Weird! But probably fine. Now I cross my fingers and hope Valve don’t kill it off in a few days’ time, like the last Steam Machine accessory I tried.

items.title: I taught an old man new tunes in rhythm-action shopkeeper sim Mr. Records, and now you can try the demo yourself
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: One of the bright spots of a miserably grey Summer Game Fest 2026 was Mr. Records, a mashup of rhythm-action autorunner and casual vinyl shop management by
items.text:
One of the bright spots of a miserably grey Summer Game Fest 2026 was Mr. Records, a mashup of rhythm-action autorunner and casual vinyl shop management by music game specialists Glee-Cheese Studio. I’ve since played a demo – which you can now try yourself on Steam – and was pleased by the apparent confirmation that it can induce that head-nodding, foot-tapping thing that rhythm games should. Big fan, usually, of games that force me into involuntary body movements.

Watch on YouTube

Mr. Records follows George, a crusty but friendly old music aficionado in the process of establishing his own records boutique. Before putting a new song on the shelves, George insists on giving it a private listen, which sinks him into fantasy platforming sequences where successful jumps, slides, and throws are exclusively made on the beat. The next morning, punters show up asking for help finding a specific record, a task to which George – head still swollen with last night’s melodic discoveries – can apply his newfound knowledge.

Of this double A-side approach, I found the rhythm component the better bop. Its 2D button-tapping keeps it simpler than a Hi-Fi Rush or Metal: Hellsinger, but the mixing-up of jumps and slides and kicks quickly establishes the action as the kind where a momentary lapse in concentration can irreparably muck up your timing. Hence, head-nodding and foot-tapping.

George’s daydreams also have their own, colourful charm, scrolling along like the Yellow Submarine video by way of Thank Goodness You’re Here. Environments take inspiration from the song they accompany, so a breezy pop number might lead you through fields of dancing pastel flowers, while a fuzzy electronic track is all purple and pulsing. Well, maybe not all, as transitions between sections of a song may have a corresponding visual or mechanical shift that lasts only for that section – potentially including George's movement orientation being flipped sideways or upside down. Which is as disorienting as trying to play a guitar back to front, but also a good sign that Glee-Cheese have engineered every step of George’s wanderings to lock in with the flow of the music.

The songs in question are also entirely original, composed and recorded in-house. They’re a diverse bunch, the tracks I played through spanning psychedelic pop, classic rock and R&B-inspired rap (among others), and most have a lyrical whimsy to them that pairs well with the cartoon visuals. There’s some decently catchy earworms in there too, though the one song that lodged itself deepest within my head was also the one I most wanted rid of: a sausage-themed comedy tune whose chestless, too-close-to-the-mic crooning was and remains the stuff of nightmares. Thankfully, the rest of the soundtrack seems to be inoffensive at worst and jolly good fun at best, and the breadth of genres bodes well for George's dreamscape variety.

The shop management/social puzzling side, I imagine, needs more time to show its stuff. It’s based around recommending the right record based on customers’ vague, partial descriptions, but in the early stages I played, the challenge of digging up the correct vinyl was undermined by a lack of stock. George’s grand opening makes all of two records available, a business plan that would probably kill Claude from The Apprentice on the spot, and it looks like you’ll only be adding one or two records per night.

Also, and this is for sure a limitation of the demo/preview format, I could only see the shoots of the shopkeeping’s relationship-building aspect. Despite the lack of choice, it seems George does pick up some repeat customers, and it sounds like cultivating friendships with the regulars may prove more important than the shop’s balance sheet.

I’m interested to see where that goes, mind, as I am for George’s own story. A greyed puffin whose primary companion is a nap-happy dog, he has the air of someone to whom life hasn’t always been kind, even as he continues to appreciate and find solace in its artistic pleasures. Fortunately, this love of music is clearly shared by the game as a whole, which is exactly what you want when half of it is spent hitting buttons to an imaginary metronome.

items.author: Brent Koepp
items.summary: A GTA 6 collector’s edition may have leaked through listings tied to the Rockstar Games Store. Fans also found references to dozens of Grand Theft Auto VI
items.text:
A GTA 6 collector’s edition may have leaked through listings tied to the Rockstar Games Store. Fans also found references to dozens of Grand Theft Auto VI merchandise items, including shirts, hats and a Burger Shot leather lunch bag.

GTA 6 Collector’s Edition May Be Called the Vice City Collection

Screenshot: Rockstar Games

Eagle-eyed fans have reportedly found a listing for GTA VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection on the Rockstar Games store website. According to the GTA Forums, some believe it could be a GTA 6 collector’s edition for the physical release of the game.

Fans spotted the listing through a store URL. The link doesn’t currently show a product page, but its files reportedly identify the item as a “physical good.” Adding to the mystery, is the Vice City Collection is reportedly around 8.6 kilograms, or 18 pounds. items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post.
